Mojang already gave us the necessary features for a functioning economy. We don't need fake plugin money to get what we want. If I want something from someone else, I get what they want, and we trade, and we both are now happier because we gained items that we wanted and lost items we didn't want as much. A bartering based economy will work better than a currency one on this server.

A bartering-only economy would be beneficial in establishing a good community. Instead of amassing mass amounts of money and clicking on a chestshop to get what I want, I have to actually interact with other players to secure a deal. We would have to make negotiations and cooperate so that everyone gets what they want. Trading is a great way to build bonds between players who normally might not interact with each other.

The origin of the money itself is not representative of everything that is valuable to players. The server shops pump money into the economy, but will only accept certain items, which give only a limited slice of all the items players could possibly produce and want. Even if every single item in the game was represented in the shops, it would impossible for the prices to be in correct proportion to each other, as supply and demand of a certain item will fluctuate. Without pegged prices of any items, prices of a certain item in relation to another will fall into its natural state, determined by the players' ability to supply it and the players' demand for it.

We should remove the currency plugin because it is damaging to the gameplay-derived vanilla economy. It makes exchange of items a lazy man's task and removes direct communication. Prices in currency will never be as good as the the players' natural prices when bartering for items. Bartering will always be better, especially on this server, which is meant to be as close to vanilla as possible. Not only is currency economy not vanilla, it's also worse than vanilla.

Personally I like both the option to barter and the option to sell/buy. Take diamonds for example, rare as hell for the most part. I dug for 3 days without finding a single one. Finally I am starting to get them, but it really is luck. What if I literally had nothing anyone wanted for their 3 diamonds so I could have a diamond pickaxe? Instead of futzing about with iron picks for the rest of my time, I could sell every bit of cobblestone I didn't need (and I have boxes and boxes of the stuff) that I had mined and then I could buy the diamonds.

You can only sell/buy limited items on that board. You still need to barter or trade with someone to get lapis, redstone, wool, meat, seeds, iron, gold, (I am partial to andesite). The only reason I am going to use the server currency is to turn my rubbish into some diamonds for my equipment. Apart from that I will barter or give away whatever another person needs. -No_Town

When you convert your crap to money, you are generating value that shouldn't be there. If nobody would normally want your cobblestone, why should they when all you've done is convert the crappy items into money? The server is pegging items to an unnatural price.

So, instead of removing a wealth of needless items, we should just have them sit around in chests or build some big pointless object? At least in turning the items into something useful, then using that item until it breaks, something good comes out if it.

Not only that, but the time someone puts into mining all that cobble is worth something, and one could consider turning that time spent into diamonds is worth it.

Except I don't want to keep asking around to see if anybody is looking to trade (which most of the time they're not) I just want to go to a location get what I want and leave, which money plugins allow.

Also, nothing is stopping you from trading with the money plugin anyway.

I'm in the mind set of having both systems. For well established members trading is a really good tool to be used like you have expressed. For the new members or those who are just new to minecraft in general it's hard to gauge what is somethings "value". The currency system would make being taken advantage of in the early times less likely as a value is already placed through the chest system.

Also, if no one is on or someone leaves then they can still make that sale. If it's a chest system that has Item A for Item B, then it's redundant because you still need another item. So you would have to harvest to get the item you really wanted without having to harvest/xp. If you use only one item for trade like diamonds, then you just replaced money for diamonds which is the same aspect.

In real life trade/bartering system can work by itself, you can't log off the /outside server and if you do your stuff goes to someone else anyways who is on the server (/s). On MC I feel we need a support system like a currency and things that still make something available when owners are offline.

While I personally agree with you, I think that this is too complex of an issue to be able to make any kind of accurate prediction.
Are there any studies on either side that point to at least some evidence?

Well, using Minimum wage data from ncsl.org and combining it with unemployment data from bls.gov we get this very oversimplified graph of wage verses unemployment rate. It does seem that as wages increase so does unemployment.

However, this overlooks a number of factors that contribute to unemployment. Cost of living, population distribution, economic history, and many other factors have all come together to create that simple graph and it would be naive to assume that the two factors were related in such a simple manner.

For many states, setting a federal $15 minimum wage would almost double their current minimum wage. This is a drastic change to adjust to (even considering that the wage would be increased over time), and there really isn't anything to compare it to. This makes it almost impossible to predict, with any certainty, how companies (and the people in those companies) will react.

Because the effects of raising minimum wage are so complicated, it is very hard to pin down any outcomes with any real certainty. This is why there are so many differing opinions. One the one side there are people who believe and can model scenarios where an increase would destroy the economy. On the other people who can show a significant increase in economic growth. I'm guessing it's somewhere in the middle.
Somewhere in the middle makes sense. Are there any studies or reports you'd recommend?

Freakanomics has a short summary of a paper written by Jeremy Magruder. Magruder's paper gives a good overview of what happened in Indonesia, and could be used to help understand what might happen in the US, but there's plenty of room for speculation.
